seoDesc: MCA perinatology: work out moM from the MCA peak systolic velocity. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The MCA perinatology calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports moM immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the MCA perinatology calculator work?
sections.html:
The MCA perinatology calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports moM in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the gestational age and the gestational age (2)); then you type in the MCA peak systolic velocity and the MCA peak systolic velocity (2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the MCA perinatology calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Mo m=(MCA peak systolic velocity ÷ median peak systolic velocity)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The MCA perinatology calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the MCA peak systolic velocity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the MCA perinatology calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns moM, derived from the MCA peak systolic velocity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the MCA perinatology calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the MCA peak systolic velocity, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter MCA peak systolic velocity in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. MCA peak systolic velocity opens in centimeters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Median peak systolic velocity = 0 cm/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the MCA perinatology calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
